analysis.one_liner: Conditions nonprofit hospitals' tax exemption on providing substantial charity care, with a tax on shortfalls.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in September 1990 and sent to a health subcommittee, where it died in January 1991 without a vote and without a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Nonprofit hospitals are exempt from federal, state, and local taxes because they serve a charitable purpose, but the law sets no specific amount of charity care they must provide. This bill would have set specific tests: each tax-exempt hospital would have to serve Medicare and Medicaid patients openly and spend at least 50% of the value of its tax break on free or discounted care, plus 35% on other community benefits. Hospitals that fell short would pay an excise tax equal to the shortfall, and that money would flow back to states as extra Medicaid payments.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income and uninsured people who depend on hospital charity care, and state Medicaid programs, which would receive the excise-tax revenues as additional payments for hospital services. Medicare and Medicaid patients would benefit from an open-door requirement that tax-exempt hospitals not turn them away.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured patients and state Medicaid programs

how_it_helps.text: Requires each hospital operated by a tax-exempt organization to have an open-door policy toward Medicare and Medicaid patients and to serve a reasonable number of them without discrimination [S3].
Conditions the tax exemption on providing unreimbursed charity care equal to at least 50% of the value of the hospital's exemption, plus community benefits equal to 35% [S2] [S3].
Imposes an excise tax on hospitals with a charity-care shortfall, and directs the revenue to states as additional Medicaid payments for hospital services [S3].

Requires annual reporting of charity-care costs, Medicare and Medicaid patient counts, and a statement from a state official on the hospital's compliance, and requires state review of new applications for tax-exempt status [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tax-exempt hospitals, which would either spend more on free and discounted care or pay an excise tax on the shortfall; those costs could be partly reflected in prices charged to paying patients and insurers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nonprofit hospitals with low charity care

drawbacks.text: The central standard is a Treasury-estimated 'value of exempt status' tied to national averages, with adjustments so that at least 75% of tax-exempt hospitals qualify — a design the bill itself concedes is difficult, by directing Treasury to develop the measurement methodology only after two years and report on feasibility [S3].
The definition of charity care counts bad debts and shortfalls in Medicaid reimbursement, which hospitals' critics have argued can overstate the amount of genuinely free care provided [S3].
Hospitals would face detailed annual reporting requirements, including documentation and statements from state Medicaid officials, adding administrative burden [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The trade is real and substantial: tax-exempt hospitals receive large public subsidies through forgone taxes, and this bill would have converted that subsidy into a measurable, enforceable obligation to care for the poor and uninsured, with shortfall revenues recycled into Medicaid. The weaknesses are in design rather than intent — the compliance yardstick was estimated, adjustable, and partly built from bad debts, which could let hospitals count losses as charity. Still, it was the kind of specific, enforceable standard that the law at the time lacked entirely.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 1990, referred jointly to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, then sent to the Energy and Commerce health subcommittee, and never advanced before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Roybal introduced the bill on September 21, 1990, with no cosponsors [S1] [S4].
It was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S5].
On October 8, 1990, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, and no further action was taken before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tax-exempt hospitals keep their exemptions without a defined charity-care obligation; low-income and uninsured patients gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nonprofit hospitals kept their exemptions unchanged

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 21, 1990 and chaired no committee action on it; it died in committee.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 21, 1990 and took no action on the bill before the Congress ended.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 21, 1990 and sent it to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment on October 8, where it remained without further action.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors, so there is no record of where members other than the sponsor stood.

industries.note: These hospitals receive large tax subsidies in exchange for a charitable purpose the law leaves undefined; the bill would have quantified the obligation in dollars and taxed the shortfall. Ordinary people pay those forgone taxes and often rely on the charity care the bill would have required.

By attaching a measurable standard to the nonprofit exemption, the bill would have narrowed the competitive advantage tax-exempt hospitals hold over for-profit ones. The benefit to the public runs through fairer competition, not directly.
Excise taxes collected from hospitals in each state would have been returned as additional federal Medicaid payments for hospital services, easing state budgets and care for Medicaid patients.
